thread.title_full: Students call for divestment on anniversary of Oct. 7 attacks

author: Alaine Hanson
title: Students call for divestment on anniversary of Oct. 7 attacks
text:
More than 100 people chanted “Regents, regents, you can’t hide, we charge you with genocide” throughout the University of Michigan campus Wednesday afternoon in a walkout marking three years since Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023 attack on Israel.
The protest — organized by Students Allied for Freedom and Equality — called for the University to divest from its financial and academic relationships with Israel.
Protesters started at the President’s House, looping onto State Street and ending in front of the Central Campus Transit Center. Other chants included “From the river to the sea, Palestine will be free; from the sea to the river, Palestine will live forever” and “Israel bombs, U of M pays, how many kids did you kill today?”
The walkout encouraged students to continue organizing despite the University’s history of punishing pro-Palestine activism on campus. To open the walkout, SAFE’s co-president, who was masked and remained anonymous, reflected on the recent history of pro-Palestine activism at the University — including the 2024 encampment and graduation disruptions — which were met with police violence and criminal charges against protesters . She said these challenges have only strengthened their support.
“This repression has only taken place because we have made our movement impossible to ignore, and because of the change we are creating,” SAFE’s co-president said. “We will respond to every arrest, every charge, every surge of repression with stronger resistance and greater collective power.”
During the Oct. 7 attack, Hamas killed more than 1,200 people and took more than 250 hostage. Israel’s subsequent military campaign in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 people and was classified as a genocide by the United Nations
SAFE’s co-president reaffirmed SAFE’s call for divestment, saying the University needs to end collaboration with Israel.
“Our university tries to convince us that academic and financial partnerships with Israel are nothing but standard business — that they are promoting open dialogue and democracy,” she said. “However, we know that there is no rational reason for our university endowment to fund collaboration with the state that is actively participating in genocide.”
Rackham student Nia D. Hall spoke next, saying Palestinian solidarity connects to historic U.S. struggles like the Black liberation and workers’ rights movements.
“These struggles may not be identical, but they are connected,” Hall said. “They are connected by the questions of who gets to make decisions, whose consent matters, whose speech is protected, what resistance is criminalized, whose land can be taken, whose communities can be sacrificed and whose lives institutions decide are acceptable collateral damage.”
The third speaker, who remained anonymous and wore his grandfather’s keffiyeh, focused on Palestinian resistance and the role of speech in activism. He contrasted his grandfather’s physical resistance in the First Intifada with his verbal resistance in peaceful protests. Pointing to the police presence around campus during the walkout as evidence of the power of student speech and organizing, he said students’ ability to speak publicly about Palestine was itself a form of political power.
“Our words are dangerous to this university,” he said. “They are dangerous to the United States, and they are dangerous to the world because we can tell people how we feel, we can tell people what is wrong with this world and we can make change.”
Daily Staff Reporter Alaine Hanson can be reached at alaineh@umich.edu .
